_source: Generated from the GhanaCropGuard AI Python backend (knowledge.py, labels.py, schemas.py, inference.py). This file is now the source of truth; follow docs/CONTENT_POLICY.md in the ghanacropguard-ai repo when editing guidance.
disclaimer: This is an AI-assisted preliminary assessment, not a diagnosis. It can be wrong. Confirm with an agricultural extension officer before acting.

warningText.low_confidence: The model is not confident about this photo. Treat the result as a weak hint and consult an extension officer.
warningText.close_alternatives: Two or more conditions scored similarly. Check the alternatives listed.
warningText.crop_uncertain: The model is unsure which crop this is. Make sure the photo shows cashew, cassava, maize or tomato.
warningText.low_resolution: The photo is small. A closer, sharper photo of the affected part may give a better result.
warningText.scope: This tool only recognises 22 conditions of cashew, cassava, maize and tomato. Other crops or problems will still be matched to one of these, so results for anything else are not meaningful.

mofa.title: Ministry of Food and Agriculture, Ghana

alwaysSteps: Check several plants across the field, not just one leaf, before deciding anything.
If you are unsure, or the problem is spreading, show the plant to your district MoFA agricultural extension officer.
escalate: Contact your district agricultural extension officer (Ministry of Food and Agriculture) for confirmation and for advice on any approved crop-protection products.

cashew_anthracnose.summary: Anthracnose is a fungal disease of cashew (commonly Colletotrichum species). It is favoured by warm, humid or rainy weather and attacks young leaves, flowers and nuts.
signs: Reddish-brown to dark, sunken patches on young leaves, shoots, flowers or nuts
Affected flowers and young nuts may dry and fall
steps: Prune and remove badly affected shoots and fallen infected material from the farm
Open up the canopy by pruning so air can move and leaves dry faster
Keep the area under the trees clean

cashew_gummosis.summary: Gummosis is a disease in which the cashew tree oozes gum from the bark of the trunk or branches. It is commonly associated with fungal infection (e.g. Lasiodiplodia theobromae), often entering through wounds.
signs: Gum oozing from cracks on the trunk or branches
Darkened, cracked bark (cankers)
Branch dieback in severe cases
steps: Avoid wounding trunks with tools or fire
Remove and safely dispose of dead branches
Ask an extension officer to inspect trees with large cankers

cashew_healthy.summary: No signs of the cashew conditions this model was trained on were detected in this photo.
steps: Keep monitoring, especially during new leaf flushes and flowering
Maintain good field hygiene and pruning

cashew_leaf_miner.summary: The cashew leaf miner is a small moth whose larvae feed inside young, tender leaves, leaving blister-like mines.
signs: Silvery or pale blisters/patches on young leaves
Young leaves may curl, dry or tear
steps: Watch new leaf flushes closely, when attack is most likely
Remove and destroy heavily mined shoots on small trees
Encourage natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary broad spraying

cashew_red_rust.summary: Red rust on cashew is caused by a parasitic alga (Cephaleuros species) that forms rust-coloured patches, mainly in humid conditions.
signs: Small, round, orange to rusty-red velvety spots on leaves
Spots can merge in shaded, humid canopies
steps: Prune to reduce shade and humidity in the canopy
Remove heavily affected leaves and branches

cassava_bacterial_blight.summary: Cassava bacterial blight is caused by a bacterium (Xanthomonas) that spreads mainly through infected stem cuttings, rain splash and tools.
signs: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown
Leaf wilting and blight
Gum on stems and shoot dieback in severe cases
steps: Plant only cuttings taken from healthy-looking plants
Uproot and destroy badly infected plants
Clean cutting tools between fields
Rotate with a different crop

cassava_brown_spot.summary: Brown leaf spot is a fungal disease of cassava leaves. It usually affects older leaves and is often of moderate importance.
signs: Small brown spots with a darker border on older leaves
Older leaves may yellow and drop
steps: Remove fallen infected leaves
Use tolerant varieties recommended in your area
Keep plant spacing that allows air movement

cassava_green_mite.summary: Cassava green mite is a tiny pest that sucks sap from young leaves. Damage is usually worse in the dry season.
signs: Yellowish speckling on young leaves
Small, deformed leaves and stunted shoot tips
steps: Plant early in the rainy season so plants are strong before the dry season
Use tolerant varieties
Natural enemies such as predatory mites help keep numbers down, so avoid unnecessary spraying

cassava_healthy.summary: No signs of the cassava conditions this model was trained on were detected in this photo.
steps: Keep monitoring young leaves
Continue using clean planting material

cassava_mosaic.summary: Cassava mosaic disease is caused by viruses spread by whiteflies and by planting cuttings from infected plants. It is one of the most damaging cassava diseases in Africa.
signs: Yellow and green mosaic pattern on leaves
Twisted, distorted or reduced leaves
Stunted plants
steps: Plant cuttings only from healthy plants or certified clean sources
Uproot infected plants early, before they spread the virus
Use resistant varieties recommended by MoFA or research institutes

maize_fall_armyworm.summary: Fall armyworm is a caterpillar pest that feeds inside the maize whorl and on leaves. Early detection makes a big difference.
signs: Ragged holes and 'window panes' in leaves
Sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the whorl
Caterpillars in the funnel of young plants
steps: Scout the field at least weekly, especially in the first weeks after planting
Crush egg masses and young caterpillars by hand on small farms
Report outbreaks to your extension officer, who can advise on approved control options

maize_grasshopper.summary: Grasshoppers chew maize leaves. Occasional damage is common; large numbers can strip plants.
signs: Irregular chewed edges on leaves
Grasshoppers visible on or near plants
steps: Keep field borders free of tall weeds where grasshoppers shelter
Monitor numbers; report unusually large swarms to MoFA

maize_healthy.summary: No signs of the maize conditions this model was trained on were detected in this photo.
steps: Keep scouting weekly, especially for fall armyworm in young maize

maize_leaf_beetle.summary: Leaf beetles feed on maize leaves by scraping or chewing, leaving small holes or stripes.
signs: Small holes, scraped stripes or 'skeletonised' patches on leaves
Beetles on leaves
steps: Monitor how many plants are affected
Control weeds around the field
Ask an extension officer if damage is widespread on young plants

maize_leaf_blight.summary: Leaf blight of maize is a fungal leaf disease (for example northern leaf blight). It spreads in cool, humid weather and survives on crop residue.
signs: Long, grey-green to tan, cigar-shaped lesions on leaves
Lesions can join and kill leaves
steps: Rotate maize with a non-cereal crop
Manage or bury infected crop residue after harvest
Use tolerant varieties recommended in your area

maize_leaf_spot.summary: Leaf spot of maize covers several fungal diseases that form spots on leaves (for example grey leaf spot or Curvularia leaf spot).
signs: Small round or rectangular spots on leaves, often with a lighter centre or a halo
steps: Rotate crops and manage residue
Avoid very dense planting
Use tolerant varieties

maize_streak_virus.summary: Maize streak disease is caused by a virus spread by small leafhoppers. Young plants that are infected early suffer the most.
signs: Narrow, broken yellow streaks running along the leaf veins
Stunted young plants
steps: Use streak-resistant maize varieties
Avoid planting new maize next to older, infected maize
Pull out infected young plants early

tomato_healthy.summary: No signs of the tomato conditions this model was trained on were detected in this photo.
steps: Keep checking lower leaves and new growth regularly

tomato_leaf_blight.summary: Leaf blight of tomato is caused by fungal or fungus-like pathogens (for example early blight). It spreads in warm, wet conditions and starts on lower leaves.
signs: Brown spots, sometimes with rings like a target, on older leaves
Yellowing around spots and leaf drop from the bottom up
steps: Remove infected lower leaves and destroy them away from the field
Water at the base of plants, not over the leaves
Stake plants and rotate crops

tomato_leaf_curl.summary: Tomato leaf curl is usually caused by viruses spread by whiteflies. Infected plants cannot be cured, so prevention is key.
signs: Leaves curl upward and become small, thick and yellowish
Stunted plants with few fruits
steps: Remove and destroy infected plants early
Raise seedlings under insect-proof netting
Use tolerant varieties and control weeds that host whiteflies

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Septoria leaf spot is a fungal disease of tomato leaves that spreads by rain splash.
signs: Many small round spots with dark edges and grey centres on lower leaves
Tiny black dots inside the spots
steps: Remove infected lower leaves
Avoid overhead watering and working among wet plants
Rotate crops and clear plant debris after harvest

tomato_verticillium_wilt.summary: Verticillium wilt is a soil-borne fungal disease that blocks the water vessels of the plant.
signs: Yellowing, often V-shaped, on lower leaves
Wilting during the hottest part of the day
Brown discolouration inside the lower stem when cut
steps: Rotate with non-host crops such as cereals
Remove and destroy wilted plants
Use varieties listed as resistant to Verticillium
